why_wrong: Appetite defines a target risk ceiling; it doesn't address the missing granularity between ad hoc and well-managed programs
Controls gap measures a quantity of risk removed by safeguards — a different metric than program maturity
Residual risk is what remains after treatment on a single risk, not a description of how mature the overall program's processes are

questions.stem: A security awareness program reports 98% completion of annual training as its primary success metric to the board. Phishing simulation click-through rates, meanwhile, have not improved in three years. Which assessment is most accurate?
options: The program is succeeding, since completion rate is the standard measure of awareness program effectiveness
The program is succeeding, because stagnant click-through rates show the baseline threat level hasn't changed
The program should be considered a failure and cancelled, since click-through rates haven't improved at all
The program's effectiveness is unproven — completion measures delivery, not behavior change, and the flat click-through trend suggests the training isn't changing outcomes
questions.explanation: Completion rate measures delivery, not effectiveness; the flat click-through trend over three years is a behavior-metric signal that the program isn't changing outcomes.
why_wrong: Completion rate answers 'was training delivered,' not 'did behavior change' — the exam explicitly rejects treating delivery as proof of effectiveness

Flat click-through despite ongoing training is evidence the training isn't moving the needle, not evidence that the threat itself is unchanged — phishing volume/sophistication typically shifts over three years regardless
Cancelling isn't the ISC2-preferred response to underperformance — the better move is to revise the program's methods/content, not eliminate awareness training entirely

questions.stem: After a phishing simulation, a department head proposes publicly listing every employee who clicked the link and docking their annual bonus, arguing this is the fastest way to change behavior. A security awareness lead objects. What is the strongest basis for the objection?
options: Publicly listing results could violate employee privacy regulations in some jurisdictions
Bonus decisions are outside the security team's authority to influence
Phishing simulations should train and inform rather than punish, since punitive framing tends to discourage future reporting and damages security culture
The simulation results are statistically invalid unless every employee received the identical phishing template
questions.explanation: ISC2's preferred framing treats phishing simulations as training tools; punitive consequences discourage self-reporting and damage the security culture the program is meant to build.
why_wrong: A real secondary concern in some cases, but not the core security-program reason to object — the primary issue is behavioral, not a compliance technicality
True organizationally, but this argues procedure/authority, not the substance of why punitive framing is the wrong approach for a security-awareness program
Template consistency affects experimental rigor, not the ethical/behavioral objection to punishing people who click

questions.stem: A company's security awareness training has used the same slide deck and phishing examples since it was created five years ago, covering only email-based social engineering. Which gap does the periodic-content-review expectation address?
options: The training should be translated into additional languages to reach more employees
The training content should be refreshed to keep pace with emerging techniques and technologies beyond what was relevant five years ago
The training should add gamification elements to increase completion rates
The training should be shortened, since five-year-old material indicates the original version was too long to maintain
questions.explanation: Periodic content review exists specifically to keep training current with emerging threats/technologies — five-year-old, email-only content has fallen behind.
why_wrong: Translation addresses accessibility/reach, not staleness of content relative to current threats
Gamification is an engagement technique (a 'methods' concern), not the content-currency issue the scenario describes
Length has no logical connection to why content wasn't updated in five years — the gap is currency of content, not verbosity
